anchors.fact: He came from the club world, where he could turn out seven vodka drinks in fifteen seconds. On his first visit to a slow New York craft bar he was handed a Daiquiri served up, and he'd never had anything like it. Yet, in Simonson's telling, he didn't think the place would amount to much: a quarter of an hour for one round seemed laughable. He offered to bartend there one night a week anyway, to give Petraske a break, thinking he might learn something (*Proper* pp. 92–93; F3–F4).
anchors.meaning: Won over before he won anyone over. He knew the replacement from the inside before he argued for it.
anchors.speaksTo: who this is: had the replacement ready before the argument was over

anchors.fact: In 2007 The Violet Hour opened with him behind the bar, in a city Simonson sums up as beer, whiskey and nothing fancy. It had no vodka, no olives, small coupes, house rules of manners, and in his words "everything fresh, everything measured right". A month later the Drawing Room opened, and between them Chicago suddenly had a cocktail scene (*Proper* pp. 280–282; Oxford pdf 522; F6–F11).
anchors.meaning: A real overturning of how a city drank, and not done alone.

anchors.fact: Looking back, he says they had to be serious at the start, and that without that seriousness he doesn't think "this" would exist. The page doesn't say what "this" is (*Proper* p. 282; F12).
anchors.meaning: He doesn't apologise for the strictness. He liked holding the line and still says it was needed. Our reading: "this" is what Chicago's bars became.
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: likes being in charge, and always did

anchors.fact: He hired the bar's staff (Mike Ryan, 2008), and Charles Joly says Chicago's bartending family trees split into two: Bridget Albert's protégés and Toby's (*Proper* p. 283; F13–F14).
anchors.meaning: He stayed for the dull part, so the change had people to carry it.
anchors.speaksTo: gift: makes change real, still there on Monday

anchors.fact: Looking back, he cringes at some of what he did then, such as refusing to make a vodka Martini because he thought it beneath him (*Proper* p. 282; F12), when he'd once made vodka drinks by the seven (F3).
anchors.meaning: The irony, told kindly and by him first. Our reading: the one who changed how a city drank once turned down what it ordered.

anchors.fact: One of his protégés went back to his home city and co-wrote a small, self-published book, a reaction (in his co-author's words) to how boring a lot of cocktail bartenders were, with bitters and bitter liqueurs at the base of the drink. Maloney was among the bartenders who contributed to it (*Proper* pp. 283, 286–287; F15–F17).
anchors.meaning: When the next rebels came, he was in their book. The page doesn't say what he gave.
anchors.speaksTo: fear → position: ask what they'd put in its place, and listen

anchors.fact: That book's Gunshop Fizz began from The Violet Hour's Pimm's Cup template of muddled strawberry and cucumber, with Peychaud's bitters where the Pimm's had been (*Proper* p. 289; F18, F25).
anchors.meaning: The challengers kept his template and changed the heart of it.

anchors.fact: Pimm's No. 1 is a bottled gin cup: in Oxford's words essentially a bottled British Gin Sling, minus the citrus and the fizz. Only its 1912 trademark is confirmed, and no document shows James Pimm made it (Oxford pdf 1514; F21–F22).
anchors.meaning: The template was itself an old order the rebel's bar kept and served.
anchors.speaksTo: the old way kept inside the new one (Tomás's shape 2)

anchors.fact: A Pimm's Cup is customarily served tall, lengthened with lemonade or soda (Oxford pdf 1514); *Joy* builds it with 5 to 7 oz of soda, and the more traditional English way garnishes it with a sliver of cucumber (pdf 365–366). The Violet Hour's small coupes (*Proper* p. 282) are only an image prop now.
anchors.meaning: The guest's old order, served the way it has long been served. Never vodka in this pour: that was the bar's first line.

anchors.fact: Peychaud's is a bright-red bitters with a secret recipe. Oxford describes anise, nutmeg and clove *notes*, not listed ingredients (pdf 1502). It's the bottle that took the Pimm's place in the protégés' drink (*Proper* p. 289).
anchors.meaning: One spoonful of the next one's change, let into the guest's own glass.
anchors.speaksTo: fear → position: the drink as proof

anchors.fact: Clapping a sprig once between the hands to release its scent was pioneered by Maloney, "a showman's flourish" (Oxford pdf 1853).
anchors.meaning: What the old hand brings to the next one's drink (our reading; never what he gave the book, A5).
anchors.speaksTo: gift: give them something towards it

cocktail.closingLine: Spoon the bitters in before the soda. When the next one comes, ask what they'd put in its place.
method: Put the strawberries and cucumber slices in the bottom of the Collins glass with the lemon juice, and press them with a muddler until the strawberries are pulp.
Add the Pimm's, then spoon in the Peychaud's.
Fill the glass with ice, top with the soda water, and stir gently, lifting the fruit up from the bottom.
Lay the mint sprig on one palm and clap your hands together once, just hard enough to release its smell without tearing it. Set it in the glass beside a cucumber slice.
cocktail.name: Had to Be Serious

recipe.item: Pimm's No. 1 Cup, recommended, or any gin-based fruit cup of about 25%
recipe.note: The cup the template was built on.

recipe.item: Peychaud's bitters, recommended, or a bright-red aromatic bitters
recipe.note: The bitters the next book swapped in for the Pimm's. Here they go in beside it.

cocktail.tagline: You didn't just tear it down. You stayed to run it.

reading.epigraph: In one rebel drink, these bitters replaced the Pimm's. In this glass, they share it.
whoYouAre: You were the one who said the old way was finished. People laughed. Then they let you try, it worked, and the new way was yours to keep going: the rota, the budget, the wet Tuesday when nobody remembers why anything changed. Most people who start a fight are gone by then. You stayed.

You'd rarely admit it, but you never wanted a free-for-all. You wanted it run properly, by you, and you had the plan for afterwards before the argument was over. The day you dread is someone new standing where you stood, saying what you said, and you hearing yourself answer the way they once answered you. But staying is the hard part, and hardly anyone thanks you for it. You make the better way real, and keep it real, so the people who wanted it actually get to live in it.
yours: Toby Maloney came from the club world, where he could turn out seven vodka drinks in fifteen seconds. A tiny New York bar where one round took fifteen minutes struck him as laughable. He took a night a week behind its bar anyway, thinking he might learn something.

In 2007, The Violet Hour opened with him behind the bar, in Chicago, then mostly a city of beer and whiskey. Later, one bartender said the city's bartending family trees ran back to two people, and he was one.

He has since said he cringes at some of it, like refusing to make a vodka Martini because he thought it was beneath him. He also said he doesn't think any of this would exist without that seriousness. He kept both halves. A few years on, one of his protégés co-wrote a small book of radical recipes, a reaction, his co-author said, to how boring a lot of cocktail people were. Maloney contributed to it.

That's you in one life: the newcomer who laughed, the strict one who held the line, the old hand who gave something to whoever came next. You know the cringe at how hard you once had to push, and you'd still never say it was wrong to push. And one day, years in, someone younger looks at what you built the way you once looked at the old way.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from the Pimm's Cup that one of that book's recipes began with, a British summer cooler: muddled strawberry and cucumber, the Pimm's left in, a little lemon, and soda. Then one spoonful of the bright red bitters their book swapped in for the Pimm's. The measures, the lemon and one more touch are my own: a sprig of mint, clapped once between the palms, a trick Maloney pioneered, as a nod to what you bring to whatever the next one makes. Your order is still the glass. Their change is in it.

When someone you've taught comes back and tells you it's all got a bit boring, don't defend it first. Ask what they'd do instead, and give them something towards it. You had your answer ready once. So might they, and whatever they build will carry some of you in it.
